section_summary: This section begins with duplicated material on an Ibaraki conference concerning local autonomy, taxation, committee government, labor, Communist propaganda, and strained prefectural finances. It then contains a Japanese government liaison-office directory, reports on Soviet criticism of Japan’s anti-Communist policies, the termination of occupation purge machinery, local-government and land-reform problems, and proposals to restore limited Japanese control over foreign relations. The final and largest group documents major Japanese government corruption scandals—including the Arms Disposal, Showa Denko, coal-lobby, and textile cases—and assesses the reorganized Diet, procuratorial, police, and judicial mechanisms responding to them.

subfiles.title: Ibaraki Prefectural Conference on the Local Autonomy Law (concluding pages)
subfiles.about: Reports discussions at an Ibaraki prefectural conference on local finance, committee government, Communist propaganda, labor, and relations with occupation headquarters.
subfiles.summary: The concluding portion discusses proposals to transfer revenue to local governments, create a local-government bank, revise farmers’ taxes, and tax newly wealthy people. It describes Japanese uncertainty about legislative committees and occupation officers’ desire for a stronger American information program to counter Communist claims. It also records complaints about a hands-off policy toward Russians, Communist labor agitation, and delays in obtaining answers from occupation headquarters.

subfiles.title: Provincial Finances Strained
subfiles.about: Reviews the fiscal weakness and mounting obligations of Japan’s local governments.
subfiles.summary: The article states that local governments depended heavily on central subsidies and had limited independent revenue, while personnel, education, construction, and industrial-support costs consumed most of their budgets. It notes weak bond sales, the burdens of the new school system, inadequate flood-rehabilitation funds, and the difficulty of increasing taxes or Treasury support.

subfiles.title: Ibaraki Prefectural Conference on Local Autonomy Law (Chihōjichihō)
subfiles.to: Department of State, as enclosure to Despatch No. 261
subfiles.about: Provides a complete duplicate report on an occupation Government Section visit to an Ibaraki local-autonomy conference.
subfiles.summary: Japanese participants sought detailed information about American local government and expressed anxiety over inadequate prefectural revenues. Michael Nolan described proposed tax transfers, new local taxes, a local-government bank, and possible national underwriting of local deficits. Later sections address legislative committees, an American information campaign against Communist propaganda, treatment of Russians, labor disputes, and the Ibaraki Military Government Team’s frustration with headquarters delays.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 327: Directory of Central Liaison and Coordination Office
subfiles.about: Transmits five copies of the Japanese Government’s Central Liaison and Coordination Office directory.
subfiles.summary: The Acting Political Adviser forwards a directory setting out the detailed organization of the Central Liaison and Coordination Office. The directory itself follows as the enclosure.

subfiles.title: Directory of the Central Liaison and Coordination Office
subfiles.from: Central Liaison and Coordination Office, Japanese Government
subfiles.to: United States Political Adviser for Japan
subfiles.about: Lists the organization, personnel, functions, extensions, and telephone numbers of the Central Liaison and Coordination Office.
subfiles.summary: The directory identifies senior officers and the secretariat, general-affairs, liaison, local-affairs, coordination, political-economic, public-administration, war-crimes, prosecution, and investigation units. It names the chiefs and assistants responsible for relations with Allied authorities, legislation, local government, war crimes, Sugamo Prison, and related matters. Notes explain telephone extensions and the abbreviation for Local Liaison and Coordination Offices.

subfiles.title: Airgram A-572: Soviet Press on the Ashida Government
subfiles.about: Reports Soviet newspaper attacks on the Ashida government and American occupation sponsorship of Japanese anti-Communism.
subfiles.summary: Selections from Soviet press commentary accuse the Ashida Cabinet of restoring prewar reaction and preparing legislation to exclude Communists from public employment. Pravda portrays Ashida as an experienced militarist and propagandist for the Anti-Comintern Pact who rose with occupation support. It further claims that MacArthur’s supposedly democratic Japan was becoming a revived preserve of militarism.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 397: Termination of Headquarters Office on Disqualification from Public Service
subfiles.from: W. J. Sebald, United States Political Adviser for Japan
subfiles.about: Reports the abolition of SCAP’s Public Service Qualifications Division after completion of its purge-review functions.
subfiles.summary: Sebald reports that the Government Section division responsible for reviewing removal and exclusion of Japanese from public positions was abolished on June 21. Although the division ended, its personnel and records were transferred to another Government Section office. A related press release is enclosed.

subfiles.title: GHQ Press Release 1630
subfiles.from: General Headquarters, Far East Command, Public Information Office
subfiles.about: Announces repatriation totals and the abolition of SCAP Government Section’s purge machinery.
subfiles.summary: The first item reports that 5,910,861 Japanese had been repatriated, while 696,622 remained abroad, mostly in Soviet-controlled areas. The second announces that the Public Service Qualifications Division had completed its review work and was abolished after a two-and-a-half-year purge program. It supplies figures for people screened, removed, barred, provisionally designated, appealed, and reinstated.

subfiles.title: Telegram No. 1828: Soviet Coverage of Japanese Anti-Communist Measures
subfiles.about: Summarizes Soviet press treatment of an Allied Council meeting and proposed Japanese loyalty and anti-Communist legislation.
subfiles.summary: Soviet papers gave prominence to Kislenko’s Allied Council statement while sharply abbreviating Sebald’s reply. They reported proposals for loyalty checks, investigation of political activity, and removal of people allegedly obstructing economic stabilization. The telegram also notes Japanese Communist Party opposition to the proposed legislation and its calls for a peace treaty and defense of the Soviet Union.

subfiles.title: Letter Requesting Sources on Changes in Japanese Government
subfiles.to: Office of the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Requests teaching materials on changes in Japanese government under the American occupation.
subfiles.summary: Musselman explains that he will teach government at the Detroit Institute of Technology. He asks for sources covering governmental changes since the occupation began, Japan’s current relationship with the occupation, and proposed future changes.

subfiles.title: Reply to Dale T. Musselman
subfiles.from: Leonard R. Cowles, for the Acting Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Responds to Musselman’s request by enclosing material and suggesting additional government sources.
subfiles.summary: Cowles encloses documents concerning changes in Japanese government and its relations with the occupation forces. He recommends seeking further information from the Department of the Army and the Far Eastern Commission.

subfiles.title: Telegram No. 2108: Proposed Parliamentary Investigation of Communists
subfiles.about: Reports a Soviet account that Japanese parliamentary chambers planned an investigation of Communists and leftists.
subfiles.summary: A Soviet newspaper reproduced a Prague report that both houses of the Japanese Parliament had decided to create an investigative committee. Its purpose was said to be gathering testimony for a law prohibiting Communists from government posts.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 686: Problems of Local Government and Land Reform
subfiles.from: W. J. Sebald, United States Political Adviser for Japan
subfiles.about: Forwards a conversation with Kanagawa Governor Iwataro Uchiyama concerning central bureaucracy, police decentralization, and land reform.
subfiles.summary: Uchiyama complained that national agencies and their occupation counterparts were undermining local autonomy while leaving governors publicly responsible without adequate authority. He particularly criticized the expense and inefficiency of maintaining numerous separate local police forces. The despatch notes that similar objections were widespread, especially concerning public safety during major civil or labor disorders.

subfiles.title: Memorandum of Conversation: Local Government and Land Reform
subfiles.from: U. Alexis Johnson, American Consul General, Yokohama
subfiles.to: United States Political Adviser for Japan
subfiles.about: Records Governor Uchiyama’s candid assessment of administrative reform, policing, and agrarian land redistribution in Kanagawa.
subfiles.summary: Uchiyama argued that proliferating national agencies and mandated prefectural offices were weakening accountable local administration. He considered village police forces financially unsustainable and said divided authority had made policing less effective. Although land reform was broadly progressing, he described committees classifying forest and valuable beachfront property as agricultural land, causing deforestation, erosion, flood risks, and inequitable forced sales. He expected economically effective ownership eventually to gravitate toward the most enterprising farmers.

subfiles.title: Airgram No. 227: Gradual Restoration of Japanese Foreign-Relations Functions
subfiles.from: United States Political Adviser for Japan
subfiles.about: Proposes gradually allowing the Japanese Government to resume selected administrative aspects of foreign relations before a peace treaty.
subfiles.summary: The Mission observes that occupation policy denied Japan control over foreign relations and made the Political Adviser the intermediary between the Foreign Ministry and foreign missions. It recommends progressively enlarging the Foreign Office’s permissible functions so that it can acquire experience and train personnel before sovereignty is restored. The proposal calls for continued occupation supervision and requests Departmental guidance and consultation with the Supreme Commander.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on Possible Extension of Japanese Responsibility for External Relations
subfiles.from: Mr. Bond, Division of Northeast Asian Affairs
subfiles.about: Seeks a legal opinion on returning limited foreign-affairs functions to the Japanese Government.
subfiles.summary: Bond refers to Sebald’s November 1948 proposal and an attached background paper concluding provisionally that expanded Japanese responsibility would be desirable and probably feasible. He notes that the question would be reexamined in light of United States–Soviet relations. Snow is asked to identify legal impediments and ways to overcome them.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 820: Scandals in the Japanese Government
subfiles.from: W. J. Sebald, United States Political Adviser for Japan
subfiles.about: Transmits Richard B. Finn’s summary of major corruption investigations and their significance for Japanese law enforcement.
subfiles.summary: Sebald highlights scandals involving legislators, officials, government loans, military-surplus property, and millions of yen in alleged bribes. The Showa Denko investigation had already caused a cabinet’s resignation and the arrest of its former prime minister. He stresses that most major cases had not yet produced judicial findings and that the reorganized Japanese law-enforcement system was undergoing a severe test.

subfiles.title: Summary of Japanese Government Scandals
subfiles.from: Richard B. Finn, Foreign Service Officer
subfiles.to: United States Political Adviser for Japan
subfiles.about: Surveys major Japanese corruption cases and evaluates the postwar institutions investigating and prosecuting them.
subfiles.summary: Finn describes the Arms Disposal, Showa Denko, coal-lobby, Nishio, and Textile Bureau cases, tracing allegations involving missing military goods, Reconstruction Finance Bank loans, political contributions, bribery, and black-market activity. He explains the roles of the Diet’s Illegal Property Transactions Investigation Committee, public procurators, the Tokyo Metropolitan Police, and the National Rural Police. The report finds extensive corruption and administrative inefficiency but notes that investigations were exposing misconduct and testing Japan’s new legal order. It also discusses parliamentary immunity, the legal distinction between personal and party contributions, political campaign costs, inflation, and the impact of corruption on Japanese and American taxpayers.

subfiles.title: List of 34 Diet Members Arrested in 1947–1948
subfiles.to: United States Political Adviser for Japan
subfiles.about: Lists Diet members arrested or indicted in corruption cases, with party affiliations, dates, and charges.
subfiles.summary: The portion present here lists House of Representatives members implicated in the Showa Denko and coal-mine-control-bill cases. Entries identify Democratic, Democratic Liberal, New Liberal, and Social Democratic politicians accused of accepting, giving, or assisting in bribery. The page begins a third category of other cases that continues beyond this section.
